issues.description: The manuscript states that it uses social learning theory but immediately describes the stressor-emotion model of counterproductive work behavior. These are distinct frameworks with different mechanisms: observational learning/modeling versus stress appraisal/affect-driven CWB. This creates conceptual ambiguity about the hypothesized mechanism and weakens theoretical grounding.
issues.quote: To understand how incivility experiences from customers may be impacting employee affect and behavior over time, we utilize social learning theory (Bandura, 1977). This model considers how individuals learn behaviors through observation and modeling of others' actions and their consequences, ultimately shaping counterproductive work behaviors (CWB), such as enacted incivility. Applied to enacted incivility, the general premise of the model suggests that enacted incivility occurs due to a sequence of events where environmental stressors at work lead to enacted incivility through appraisal, perceptions of the stressor, and negative emotions (Spector & Fox, 2005).

issues.description: The compassion fatigue section states that the study examines coworker incivility, whereas the study hypotheses, measures, title, and analyses concern patient/customer incivility. This is not merely wording: coworker incivility and patient/customer incivility have different relational structures, power dynamics, and theoretical implications.
issues.quote: Within the current study, we look specifically at the relationship between experiencing coworker incivility and experiencing a caregiving specific form of job burnout, compassion fatigue.

issues.description: Recruitment materials specified full-time nurses in high-stakes/critical care settings, but the final sample is described as including part-time and full-time nurses. This changes the target population and may affect exposure to patients, incivility, fatigue, and acuity.
issues.quote: Information about inclusion criteria (working full time in a high-stakes/critical care setting as a nurse) and compensation were also provided along with the link to participate.

issues.description: The final sample description contradicts the stated full-time inclusion criterion by including part-time nurses. If part-time nurses were retained, the authors need to explain whether inclusion criteria changed, how many part-time participants were included, and whether work hours moderated or confounded effects.
issues.quote: All participants were currently employed as a nurse (part- or full-time), worked more than one shift a week, on average, and routinely worked with high severity/high-risk patients.

issues.subcategory: attrition arithmetic does not add up
issues.description: The wave counts imply 18 participants did not complete all four waves from Time 1 to Time 4, but the text states that only 16 were excluded for missing time points. This discrepancy undermines confidence in the sample accounting.
issues.quote: n = 468 nurses responded at time 1; n = 458 responded at time 2 (98% retention rate between T1 and T2); n = 454 responded at time 3 (98% retention rate between T2 and T3); and n = 450 responded at time 4 (98% retention rate between T3 and T4).

issues.description: The manuscript says 78 people were excluded for poor data quality, but the listed reasons account for only 57 exclusions. Twenty-one exclusions are unexplained, creating a serious reporting and reproducibility problem.
issues.quote: Responses were considered failed data quality checks if they had any of the following characteristics: (a) demographic information was not consistent across measurement periods (n = 56 people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age); or (b) missing values exceeded 50% of the questions (n = 1). This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.subcategory: final sample size inconsistent with analysis sample
issues.description: The methods report a final sample of N = 372, but the main correlation and mediation tables use N = 321, and the moderated analyses use N = 244. The loss of 51 participants before main analyses and 128 before moderation is not adequately explained, especially because Table 2 does not include the moderator.
issues.quote: This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.description: The main analytic sample is N = 321, not the reported final sample N = 372. The manuscript does not explain which variables caused the additional missingness, whether listwise deletion was used, or whether excluded cases differed from retained cases.
issues.quote: Note. N = 321. Cronbach’s α presented on the diagonal. Coefficients above |.20| significant at p < .001. *p < .05

issues.description: The moderated regression uses only N = 244, representing a large reduction from the final sample and even from the N = 321 main analytic sample. The manuscript attributes this to missingness on patient acuity but does not provide a missing-data mechanism assessment, sensitivity analysis, imputation, or comparison of retained versus excluded participants.
issues.quote: Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.description: Participants who missed one wave were not invited to later waves. This design creates forced monotone missingness and can bias longitudinal estimates if temporary nonresponse is related to workload, stress, fatigue, or incivility—precisely the constructs being studied.
issues.quote: Due to budgetary constraints, participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys (i.e., a participant who did not complete T2 survey was not sent the link for the T3 or T4 surveys).

issues.description: The reported 98% retention rates are conditional between waves and obscure the total reduction from initial respondents to analyzed cases. The effective analytic retention is much lower for the main and moderated models, which affects validity and power.
issues.quote: n = 458 responded at time 2 (98% retention rate between T1 and T2); n = 454 responded at time 3 (98% retention rate between T2 and T3); and n = 450 responded at time 4 (98% retention rate between T3 and T4).

issues.description: The manuscript reports that acuity had missing or invalid data but does not state the number or percentage missing, how invalid values were defined, whether values were recoded or deleted, or whether missingness was associated with key variables.
issues.quote: Finally, our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data. For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response).

issues.description: Patient acuity was elicited as a percentage, but Table 1 reports means as proportions. If respondents entered 50 rather than .50, responses may have been classified as invalid depending on the unspecified expected range. This likely contributed to missingness and threatens validity of the moderator.
issues.quote: what percentage of patients under your care in the past week would be considered "severe"?

issues.description: Patient acuity is operationalized with a single self-report percentage item, despite being defined as severity of illness and intensity of nursing care. A single perceived percentage does not capture acuity intensity, variability, patient count, nurse-patient ratios, or objective clinical workload.
issues.quote: we measure the respondents’ perceptions of patient acuity across all patients they attended to within the last work week by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were “severe.”

issues.description: The item asks nurses across different specialties to use their department’s own acuity scale, but different scales are not equivalent. Combining ESI, CRIB, SOIS, PRO tools, and unspecified local scales makes the moderator non-comparable across participants.
issues.quote: Some example scales include: the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), the Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), the Severity of Illness Scale (SOIS), or other patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools

issues.description: The construct is defined as patient illness severity and intensity of nursing care, but the operational measure is a subjective estimate of the proportion of severe patients. This conflates objective acuity, subjective workload, stress appraisal, and mood, making moderation effects difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: Within this study, we look at perceptions of patient acuity across all patients seen within a given work week as a potential stressor that may be exacerbating the negative effects of experienced incivility.

issues.description: Experienced incivility is described as patient incivility but the item stem includes patients and family members/friends. These sources may differ in frequency, severity, intent, and relationship to nurse outcomes. Conflating them weakens construct precision.
issues.quote: how often have you been in a situation where any of your patients or patient family members/friends…

issues.description: Enacted incivility is labeled as toward patients, but items include patient family members. Incivility toward a patient versus toward a family member has different clinical and ethical meanings and may have different antecedents.
issues.quote: Put down one or more patients/patient family members or acted condescendingly towards them

issues.description: Some enacted incivility items may reflect clinically necessary skepticism or low weighting of patient/family judgment rather than rude or deviant behavior, especially in high-acuity contexts. This threatens construct validity of enacted incivility.
issues.quote: Doubted one or more patient’s/patient family members’ judgment on a matter over which they had responsibility

issues.description: Compassion fatigue is a cumulative syndrome involving burnout and secondary trauma, but it is measured weekly with items such as sleep loss over traumatic experiences. The weekly state operationalization may not validly capture the chronic construct theorized.
issues.quote: For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week.

issues.subcategory: compassion fatigue mechanism not specific to incivility
issues.description: Compassion fatigue includes secondary trauma from patients’ traumatic experiences, which may be driven by clinical exposure rather than incivility. This makes it difficult to interpret compassion fatigue as a mechanism specifically linking incivility to enacted incivility.
issues.quote: Compassion fatigue consists of burnout and secondary trauma components, with employees experiencing compassion fatigue if they are experiencing either caregiving-related burnout or secondary trauma (or both of these simultaneously).

issues.description: The authors used selected highest-loading items from longer scales and adapted wording to patients/families, but the main study does not report item loadings, content coverage evidence, measurement invariance over time, or validation of the adapted enacted incivility scale in this population.
issues.quote: For each scale, the highest loading items were chosen from reported factor analytic data to maintain a reasonable survey length and achieve internal consistency reliability (Maloney et al., 2011).

issues.description: Participants were recruited through flyers, personal networks, social media, forums, and a hospital news forum. The sampling frame and response rate are unknown, creating strong potential for self-selection bias among nurses interested in incivility, wellbeing, or compensation.
issues.quote: Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies.

issues.subcategory: unknown response rate and sampling frame
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that the sampled population size is unknown. Without a sampling frame or response rate, representativeness and nonresponse bias cannot be evaluated.
issues.quote: Although the full population size that was sampled from is unknown

issues.description: Open recruitment through links/QR codes and social media relied on self-report to verify that participants were nurses in high-stakes settings. This is vulnerable to ineligible respondents, duplicate responses, and fraudulent participation.
issues.quote: To help ensure that the participants were from healthcare contexts, we highlighted the nursing focus in the recruitment and consent information and directly asked participants if they met the inclusion criteria.

issues.description: The manuscript says no participant emails were obtained during recruitment, but later surveys had to be sent only to prior completers. The procedure for collecting contact information, linking responses across waves, preserving confidentiality, preventing duplicate participation, and compensating participants is not described.
issues.quote: no participant emails were obtained or used during the recruitment process

issues.description: The authors state that data-quality checks were a priori but do not define what counted as “reasonably consistent” tenure, gender, or age. Excluding 56 participants on this basis without transparent thresholds creates researcher degrees of freedom and potential bias.
issues.quote: n = 56 people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age

issues.description: The study involves multiple waves, exclusions, shortened/adapted scales, missing-data decisions, controls, mediation, moderated mediation, and supplemental analyses. No preregistration or analysis plan is reported, making it difficult to distinguish confirmatory from exploratory decisions.
issues.quote: We conducted a series of supplemental analyses to 1) address unhypothesized moderation effects and 2) investigate the relationship between compassion fatigue and enacted incivility.

issues.description: No a priori power analysis or sensitivity analysis is reported for the longitudinal mediation or the moderated mediation. This is especially problematic because the moderator model uses only N = 244 and interaction/indirect effects are typically underpowered.
issues.quote: We tested our hypotheses using data collected across four waves separated by one-week lags.

issues.description: The analyses regress later variables on earlier variables but do not appear to control for prior levels of the same outcomes, such as T1/T2 negative emotions, T1/T3 compassion fatigue, or T1/T3 enacted incivility. Without autoregressive controls, coefficients may reflect stable between-person differences rather than within-person change over time.
issues.quote: We tested this hypothesis by regressing negative emotions toward patients (T3) onto experienced patient incivility (T2).

issues.description: The very high cross-time and cross-construct correlations suggest stable individual differences or response tendencies may drive associations. Without trait negative affectivity, baseline strain, personality, unit climate, or prior incivility controls, causal interpretation is not justified.

The hypothesized serial mediation requires compassion fatigue to precede enacted incivility, but both are measured at Time 4. This prevents establishing temporal ordering for the final mediation path and undermines claims that compassion fatigue leads to enacted incivility.
issues.quote: Time 3 negative emotions toward patients were positively related to Time 4 compassion fatigue

issues.subcategory: overstated causal claims from observational data
issues.description: The design is observational and self-report, with no randomization, manipulation, or strong confound control. Claims that incivility “leads to” outcomes and that the model shows a cascade are stronger than the evidence supports.
issues.quote: These findings suggest that repeated exposure to incivility leads to both poor wellbeing outcomes for the target of incivility and to future enacted incivility.

issues.description: The analytic strategy claims the longitudinal model allows stronger causal inference, but time ordering alone does not address unmeasured confounding, reverse causation, stable traits, common-method variance, or omitted autoregressive paths.
issues.quote: allows for stronger causal inferences by modeling the longitudinal effects of predictors across multiple points in time

issues.description: Theoretical and empirical incivility processes can be reciprocal: nurses who enact incivility may elicit patient/family incivility, and fatigue may influence perceptions of experienced incivility. The manuscript does not test cross-lagged or reciprocal alternatives.
issues.quote: experiencing incivility from patients was related to increased future incivility enactment towards patients indirectly through increased negative emotions towards patients and compassion fatigue

issues.description: All key constructs were reported by the same respondent using similar Likert scales. This inflates associations through common-method variance, negative response style, social desirability, and consistency motifs, especially for sensitive enacted incivility.
issues.quote: First, our data were collected using self-report questionnaires.

issues.description: Enacted incivility toward patients is socially and professionally sensitive. Self-reports may underreport actual behavior or reflect self-perception rather than behavior. No patient, family, coworker, supervisor, or observational corroboration is used.
issues.quote: Four items from the Enacted Incivility Scale (Cortina et al., 2001) were used to measure the frequency participants instigated incivility towards their patients.

issues.description: Experienced and enacted incivility use nearly identical item wording with only direction reversed. This can produce artificial correlations from item similarity rather than substantive experienced-to-enacted processes.
issues.quote: The item content for these four items was similar to the four items used in the customer incivility scale, with changes to the instructions that prompted participants to respond about how they behaved towards their patients

issues.description: Several key constructs correlate extremely highly, including compassion fatigue and enacted incivility at r = .91 and negative emotions and compassion fatigue at r = .96. These correlations raise serious concerns that the constructs are empirically indistinguishable or dominated by a general distress/common-method factor.

The very high correlations among mediators and outcome imply severe multicollinearity in regression/path models, making coefficients unstable and indirect effects difficult to interpret. The manuscript does not report VIFs, condition indices, or robustness checks.

The CFA omits the chi-square symbol, does not report p-values, factor loadings, factor correlations, alternative model fit statistics, item thresholds, or whether the model was tested across waves. The statement that alternative models fit worse is not evaluable without details.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99) and fit the data better than alternative models with fewer factors.

issues.subcategory: borderline model fit called acceptable without qualification
issues.description: RMSEA = .08 is at best borderline and the chi-square appears very large relative to df. Given extreme interconstruct correlations, stronger evidence for discriminant validity is needed before treating constructs as distinct.
issues.quote: RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99

issues.description: The manuscript says it investigated discriminant validity of the measures but tested only a four-factor model, excluding patient acuity. Because acuity is central to Hypothesis 3, its measurement validity remains untested.
issues.quote: First, we assessed our hypothesized four-factor model absent of the temporal control measures.

issues.description: The study compares and links constructs across four weekly waves, but there is no evidence that adapted scales measured the same constructs equivalently across time. Without longitudinal measurement invariance, cross-wave mediation paths may be biased.
issues.quote: Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks.

issues.description: Nurses were recruited from multiple hospitals and possibly units/departments, but analyses do not account for clustering by hospital, unit, manager, shift, or department. Shared unit climate, staffing, acuity systems, and local norms could violate independence and bias standard errors.
issues.quote: Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies.

issues.description: Although each construct was measured at every wave, the main models appear to use selected waves rather than modeling within-person trajectories, lagged change, or accumulation. This limits claims about processes unfolding over time and cumulative exposure.
issues.quote: The subsequent waves were included for hypothesis testing (see Figure 1 for information what measurement period each variable in the model was taken from).

issues.description: The theory emphasizes chronic, repeated, cumulative exposure, but the focal predictor is weekly incivility at T2 rather than cumulative exposure across weeks or a trajectory. The operationalization does not match the chronic-hassle claim.
issues.quote: we propose that it is not only important to examine events-based reactions to incivility from a single person, as much of the previous reciprocation research has done, but also how cumulative weekly exposure to incivility across customers and workdays can influence employee wellbeing and behaviors.

issues.description: Work hours appear in Tables 1–3 and in regression models, but the measure, timing, rationale, and inclusion rules for controls are not described in the Measures section. It is also unclear why some models include T2 work hours, others T3 work hours, and whether T1 controls were used.

issues.subcategory: table title claims T1 controls but models show other controls
issues.description: Table 1 is titled as using Time 1 controls, but it includes T2 and T3 work hours, and Table 2 shows T2/T3 work hours rather than T1 controls. This inconsistency makes the analytic model unclear.
issues.quote: Correlation and Descriptive Information for Hypothesized Model with Time 1 Controls

issues.description: For a serial mediation from experienced incivility to negative emotions to compassion fatigue to enacted incivility, the indirect effect should multiply all three constituent paths. The text says it was estimated by multiplying only the first and last stages, creating ambiguity about what was actually tested.
issues.quote: Here, the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying the first and last stages in the serial mediation process (a × d).

issues.subcategory: reported indirect effect SE inconsistent across text and table
issues.description: The H4 indirect effect is reported with SE = .04 in the prose but SE = .02 in Table 2. This affects inference and suggests reporting or calculation errors.
issues.quote: Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients (B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]).

issues.subcategory: supplemental regression contradicts main regression table
issues.description: The supplemental regression reports negative emotions and compassion fatigue both with B = .23, SE = .04, whereas Table 2 reports B = .28, SE = .10 for negative emotions and B = .57, SE = .17 for compassion fatigue predicting enacted incivility. The discrepancy is not explained by standardization or sample differences.
issues.quote: experienced incivility (B = -.03, SE = .04, p = .40), negative emotions (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001), and compassion fatigue (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001).

issues.description: The text says the compassion fatigue parameter is nearly six times that of negative emotions, but Table 2 shows .57 versus .28, approximately two times, and the supplemental regression shows both as .23. This undermines interpretation of the relative importance analysis.
issues.quote: As seen in Table 2, the last step of the simple mediation reflects a parameter estimate for compassion fatigue that is nearly six times that of negative emotions.

issues.description: The relative importance results sum to 100%, indicating they are proportions of explained variance, not proportions of total variance in enacted incivility. The text says each predictor accounted for that percentage of variance, which overstates the result unless explicitly tied to R².
issues.quote: The results revealed compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively.

issues.description: The manuscript does not fully specify whether mediation models were estimated using observed scale scores or latent variables, the estimator, missing-data estimator, centering of predictors for interactions, standardization of coefficients, covariance structure, or whether robust standard errors were used.
issues.quote: We then used MPlus’ model constraint feature to estimate the indirect path a × d.

issues.description: The interaction between incivility and patient acuity is central to Hypothesis 3, but the manuscript does not report whether variables were mean-centered or standardized, how low/medium/high values were defined beyond Figure 3, or how the product term was constructed.
issues.quote: Results revealed that the Time 2 experienced incivility × Time 2 perceived patient acuity interaction term was significant (B = .34, SE = .12, p < .01).

issues.description: Tables 2 and 3 contain duplicated headers, blank columns, repeated notes, missing or confusing R² entries, and misaligned coefficients. This makes it difficult to reconstruct the models or verify results.
The confidence interval for the index of moderated mediation is missing a closing bracket, indicating poor statistical reporting and making exact interval extraction ambiguous.

The supplemental analyses show that the conditional indirect effects and index of moderated mediation were nonsignificant, yet the discussion implies that high patient acuity exacerbates the full downstream pathway to fatigue and behavior. The evidence supports only moderation of the first-stage association, not the indirect effect.
issues.quote: Taken together, these results reveal the indirect effect is not conditional upon perceived patient acuity.

issues.description: The discussion suggests that simultaneous incivility and patient acuity increase risk of fatigue and enacted incivility, but the moderated mediation test did not support conditional indirect effects. This overstates the moderation findings.
issues.quote: nurses are at increased risk of the negative emotional processes and behaviors when they are simultaneously experiencing interpersonal (i.e., experienced customer incivility) and task-related (i.e., perceived patient acuity) stressors.

issues.description: The manuscript claims nurses experiencing more patient incivility are more likely to enact incivility, but the direct path from T2 customer incivility to T4 enacted incivility controlling mediators is nonsignificant and negative in Table 2, and the total effect is not reported. The claim should be limited to the reported indirect association.

The discussion recommends targeted interventions based on observational associations. Without causal identification, it is unclear whether reducing experienced incivility, negative emotions, or compassion fatigue would reduce enacted incivility.
issues.quote: Organizations should identify who is experiencing high levels of incivility and develop support systems and interventions for these employees to stop the negative affective and energetic process our results suggest are occurring.

issues.description: The sample consists of mostly female U.S. nurses in high-stakes healthcare settings, recruited nonprobabilistically. Findings may not generalize to other service employees, lower-acuity care, non-U.S. contexts, male nurses, physicians, or non-healthcare customer service workers.
issues.quote: Using a four-wave data collection of service employees within the healthcare industry

issues.description: The abstract frames conclusions broadly as customer incivility and service work, but the empirical sample is limited to nurses and patients/families. Patients in critical care are not equivalent to ordinary customers.
issues.quote: These findings suggest that repeated exposure to incivility leads to both poor wellbeing outcomes for the target of incivility and to future enacted incivility.

issues.description: The manuscript treats patients and families as customers, but high-acuity patients may be in pain, cognitively impaired, frightened, intoxicated, traumatized, or otherwise constrained. The ethical and power dynamics of nurse-patient care differ substantially from typical customer-employee relationships, affecting interpretation of intent, incivility, and enactment.
issues.quote: We view the patient-nurse relationship as a specialized form of customer-employee relationship.

issues.subcategory: exposure not normalized by work hours or patient volume
issues.description: Weekly incivility, emotion, fatigue, and enacted incivility ratings likely depend on hours worked, number of shifts, number of patients, unit type, and patient volume. The study does not collect or adjust for patient counts, and work hours are inconsistently handled.
issues.quote: For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week.

issues.description: The study targets high-stakes settings but does not report participants’ units, specialties, shift types, patient ratios, hospital types, geographic distribution, or COVID-era context. These details are necessary to evaluate acuity, workload, incivility exposure, and generalizability.
issues.quote: The target population of this research included nurses within healthcare industries, particularly those working in high-stakes or critical care settings.

issues.description: The qualitative pilot used only six nurses from personal networks, and the quantitative pilot used MTurk nurses, whose credentials and high-stakes setting status are difficult to verify. This is limited evidence for the adapted and shortened measures, especially patient acuity.
issues.quote: The qualitative pilot consisted of n = 6 nurses who worked in critical-care units at local hospitals and were recruited from the research team’s personal networks.

issues.description: The quantitative pilot was recruited from MTurk, but the manuscript does not report verification that respondents were nurses in high-stakes settings. This weakens the validity evidence for item clarity and applicability.
issues.quote: The quantitative pilot consisted of n = 50 nurses who worked in high-stakes settings and were recruited from MTurk.

issues.subcategory: R2 implausibly high without diagnostic discussion
issues.description: The enacted incivility model reports R² = .81, extremely high for behavioral self-report data and likely driven by overlapping constructs, common method, and multicollinearity. The manuscript does not discuss this as a validity warning or report diagnostics.

Negative emotions toward patients are operationalized with four anger/frustration-related items only. This may not represent the broader negative affective mechanism theorized by the stressor-emotion model, which can include anxiety, sadness, fear, guilt, or distress.
issues.quote: The scale items consisted of four negative emotions: (a) frustration, (b) irritability, (c) anger, (d) resentment.

issues.description: The manuscript does not explicitly state whether item responses were averaged, summed, modeled as latent variables, or otherwise transformed for each scale in the substantive analyses. This affects interpretation of unstandardized coefficients.
issues.quote: Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Never) to 5 (Always).

issues.subcategory: terminology shifts among customer, patient, coworker
issues.description: The manuscript alternates among customer incivility, patient incivility, coworker incivility, and patient/family incivility. These are not interchangeable and create ambiguity about constructs, hypotheses, and generalization.
issues.quote: T1 Customer Incivility

issues.description: The analytic strategy claims a lower likelihood of third-variable effects merely because of a multiwave design. Without measuring or controlling plausible confounds, temporal spacing does not rule out third variables.
issues.quote: This method also supports a lower likelihood of third variable effects (Bliese et al., 2020; Cole & Maxwell, 2003; Duncan et al., 2004)
